The Cook Political Report's Partisan Voting Index (PVI) is a measure of how strongly a congressional district leans toward either the Democratic or Republican party. It is based on the methodology introduced by Rob Richie of the Center for Voting and Democracy in the Center's July 1997 Monopoly Politics report and is updated every two years. The PVI is calculated by looking at how every congressional district voted in the past two presidential elections combined and comparing it to the national average. The index is displayed as a letter, a plus sign, and a number, with the letter indicating the party that won the district and the number showing how many percentage points above the national average it received.

In 2022, the formula for calculating PVI values was updated to weigh the most recent presidential election more heavily.

Trans broken arm syndrome is a common form of discrimination in healthcare settings where a doctor mistakenly assumes that a trans person's medical ailments stem from their trans status or gender-affirming care. This can lead to incorrect treatment or denial of care. Trans patients often hide their trans status when visiting a doctor if their problem, such as a broken arm, isn't related to their trans status. This is especially common in rural or more conservative areas. A 2022 survey from the Center for American Progress revealed that 19 percent of trans individuals had experienced this form of discrimination in the past year.

Transgender people have the right to medical privacy. According to the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), medical providers and insurance companies are prohibited from disclosing any personal medical information including a person's transgender status. HIPAA also allows transgender people to access and receive a copy of their medical records from health care facilities.

However, it can be difficult for transgender people to find insurance coverage for their medical needs. Even though there is medical consensus that hormone therapy and sex reassignment surgery (SRS) are medically necessary for many transgender people, the kinds of health care associated with gender transition are sometimes misunderstood as cosmetic, experimental or simply unnecessary. This has led to public and private insurance companies denying coverage for such treatment.
